claims.text: The net effect of chemical short-range order on thermal conductivity in single-phase bcc refractory high-entropy alloys is non-monotonic and governed by percolation of SRO clusters.
Below a critical SRO volume fraction, isolated SRO clusters act as point-defect-like phonon scatterers and reduce thermal conductivity.
Above the critical SRO fraction, connected SRO networks form coherent phonon-transport channels that restore or enhance thermal conductivity.
Percolation of SRO clusters reduces the density of diffuse antiphase boundaries that scatter phonons.
A single-phase bcc HfNbTaTiZr-like alloy can begin in a high-temperature random-solid-solution state while retaining the potential to develop SRO.
Cooling or annealing can produce SRO without necessarily producing long-range order.
Controlled annealing can tune SRO sufficiently to cross a cluster-percolation threshold.
The proposed regime is above 0.5 Tm while the alloy remains single-phase bcc.
Phonon transport dominates thermal conductivity in the proposed operating-temperature regime.
A suitable potential-energy surface must accurately represent both the energetic driving force for SRO and the energy cost of diffuse antiphase boundaries.
A connected network of SRO clusters changes the phonon mean-free-path distribution and available scattering phase space.
Non-percolating SRO states contain high-energy diffuse antiphase boundaries.
Percolating SRO networks create lower-scattering regions or 'phonon highways' that offset scattering by disordered regions.
Thermal conductivity reaches a minimum at an intermediate SRO concentration near the percolation threshold and subsequently increases.
At sufficiently high SRO fractions, thermal conductivity may exceed that of the random solid solution.
Serial/parallel mixing models and point-defect or Callaway-type theories predict a monotonic decrease in thermal conductivity as SRO concentration increases.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains single-phase bcc and SRO does not transform into long-range order or secondary phases.
The percolation threshold depends on alloy composition and on the interatomic potential's accuracy in predicting SRO cluster size and connectivity.
APT measurements of SRO connectivity combined with thermal-conductivity measurements across annealed samples can test whether conductivity changes coincide with percolation.
A continued monotonic decrease in thermal conductivity after measured SRO percolation would falsify the proposed conductivity-recovery mechanism.
